clue.text: All-round figure could be right

indicators.note: 'could be' suggests a possible version of the word that follows, so its letters may be rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, five letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone with a well-rounded figure might be just right, or perhaps a right-handed all-rounder at cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Girth is the measurement taken all the way round a body, the figure a tailor writes for the waist.

clue.text: It sounds almost like a simian type of warfare

indicators.note: a near match in sound means saying the next word aloud gives something close to the answer

blocks.note: a simian is an ape, and the great ape's name is said almost the same

explanation.surface: Fighting like apes, the clue jokes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' allows for the two words being pronounced only nearly the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Guerrilla warfare is irregular fighting by small independent bands, from Spanish for 'little war'.

clue.text: His work helps us improve our vocabulary or maybe get le mot juste

definitions.text: His work helps us improve our vocabulary

indicators.note: 'maybe' says the words that follow could appear in another form, so their letters may be reordered

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
surface padding: French for the exact word, completing the picture of a writer's aim

explanation.surface: A reference book helps a reader find exactly the right word.
explanation.walkthrough: Le mot juste is French for the exact word, which a thesaurus helps a writer find.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Mark Roget compiled the Thesaurus of English Words and Phrases, the standard book of synonyms.

clue.text: Mine host from the Loire perhaps

indicators.note: 'perhaps' says the words before it are only one possible form, so their letters may be reordered

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An innkeeper from the Loire valley welcomes guests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mine host' is an old jocular name for the landlord of an inn.
explanation.definitionFit: A hotelier keeps a hotel, the modern counterpart of the innkeeper traditionally greeted as mine host.

clue.text: Mehitabel's biographer was one such six-footer

blocks.note: first meaning: archy, who typed up the alley cat mehitabel's adventures in Don Marquis's columns
second meaning: a creature with six feet, an insect, not a tall person

explanation.surface: A tall biographer wrote the life of a woman named Mehitabel.
explanation.walkthrough: In Don Marquis's 'archy and mehitabel', mehitabel the alley cat's doings are typed up by archy, a cockroach. 'Six-footer' reads as a tall man but means an insect.
explanation.definitionFit: Archy, the insect typist in Don Marquis's newspaper columns, chronicled the cat; insects have six legs, hence six feet.

clue.text: Captain's favourable report on colonel

blocks.note: CO is commanding officer, often a colonel
an approving okay

explanation.surface: A captain gives a good report on his colonel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' puts the report after the colonel. The captain is the 18th-century navigator who charted the Pacific.
explanation.definitionFit: James Cook was a Royal Navy captain and explorer, known always by his naval rank.

clue.text: Pin-up girl's confection

definitions.note: read as 'Pin-up girl is', a noun

blocks.note: first meaning: glamour photographs of attractive women
second meaning: a sweet dessert on a biscuit base

explanation.surface: A pin-up model's favourite pudding.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang uses the word for photographs of scantily dressed models, and it also names the rich dessert of cream cheese on crumbs.

clue.text: No new programme about fuel

blocks.note: re means concerning
peat is burnt as fuel

explanation.surface: There is no new broadcast about energy supplies.
explanation.definitionFit: A rerun of a TV show is broadcast again, so it is something viewers have seen before and not new.

clue.text: Strange angel in eastern parts brings surcease of pain

indicators.note: something strange is out of its usual order, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the first letter of the continent the eastern parts name
taken as written, to be rearranged
the rest of the continent's name

explanation.surface: An odd angelic visitor in the Orient brings relief from suffering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eastern parts' gives ASIA, split after its first A to hold the rearranged angel. Surcease is an old word for ending.
explanation.definitionFit: Analgesia is the medical term for absence of feeling of hurt, the state that painkillers produce.

clue.text: The multitude includes a trainee composer

indicators.note: to include is to take inside, so one word holds the other

blocks.note: a host is a large crowd; it splits to hold the other piece
L for learner, as on British L-plates
the last letter of host

explanation.surface: A big orchestra has a student composer among them.
explanation.definitionFit: Gustav Holst was the English composer of The Planets suite, writing in the early twentieth century.

clue.text: But one over the number involved is not needed to make them reel

definitions.text: But one over the number involved is not needed to make them reel

blocks.clueFragment: one over the number involved is not needed to make them reel
blocks.note: surface reading: one drink too many is not needed to make people stagger
setter's reading: the count of dancers in a Scottish reel, which one more than that number would spoil

explanation.surface: No need for one drink too many to set them reeling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One over the eight' is British slang for one drink too many; here the reel is the Scottish dance for eight people, so a ninth dancer is not needed.
explanation.definitionFit: An eightsome is a Scottish reel danced by a set of eight people, the group the clue says is complete without a ninth.

clue.text: White girl the pigs don't appreciate

blocks.note: first meaning: the silent-film heroine of 'The Perils of Pauline', whose surname was White
second meaning: the gem in the proverb about casting them before swine

explanation.surface: A pale girl goes unappreciated by the farmyard pigs.
explanation.walkthrough: Pearl White was the star of early film serials. 'Cast not your pearls before swine' is from the Sermon on the Mount: swine cannot value them.
explanation.definitionFit: Pearl White was a famous actress, and the proverb says that gems cast before swine are wasted on them.

clue.text: Chatterbox provided casus belli of fraternal strife

definitions.text: provided casus belli of fraternal strife

blocks.note: first meaning: someone who talks on and on

blocks.clueFragment: provided casus belli of fraternal strife
blocks.note: second meaning: the toy that Tweedledum and Tweedledee agreed to have a battle over

explanation.surface: A talkative person sparked a quarrel between brothers.
explanation.walkthrough: In 'Through the Looking-Glass', Tweedledum's new rattle is spoiled and the twin brothers agree to fight over it. Casus belli is Latin for the cause of a war.
explanation.definitionFit: A rattle is a person who chatters incessantly, and also the baby's toy over which Carroll's twins went to war.

clue.text: A proverbial slow mover, of course, in France

definitions.text: A proverbial slow mover, of course, in France

blocks.note: surface reading: a slowcoach, of course, and setter's reading: the creature that proverbially moves slowly
setter's reading: the word for that creature in French, where it is also a dish

explanation.surface: Naturally, the French have a famous slowcoach too.
explanation.walkthrough: The snail is the proverbial slow mover; the clue asks for the French word, which English uses for snails served as food.
explanation.definitionFit: Escargot is the French word for snail, the garden creature proverbially slow, and the name of the dish on menus.

clue.text: One calling round the river follows duck as supplier of eggs

indicators.note: going round something means surrounding it, so one word encloses another
to follow is to come after, fixing which piece goes second in the line

blocks.note: a duck is a nought in cricket, shaped like O
a caller, split after its second letter
the Po is Italy's longest river
the rest of the caller

explanation.surface: A visitor walks round the river behind a duck that lays eggs.
explanation.walkthrough: VISITOR goes round PO, and the whole follows O. 'Follows' means it comes after the duck.
explanation.definitionFit: An ovipositor is the tube-like organ with which a female insect or fish deposits eggs, so it supplies them.

clue.text: Pretended deference, giving cheek at the office

blocks.note: lip is insolent talk, as is cheek
an office is a church service, such as the daily office

explanation.surface: A cheeky underling mocks the boss with fake respect at work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Office' looks like a workplace, but here it means a religious rite.
explanation.definitionFit: Lip-service is respect or support expressed in words only, insincere loyalty with nothing behind it.

clue.text: Like country-lovers — being so inadequate according to Edith

definitions.text: being so inadequate according to Edith

blocks.note: first meaning: devoted to one's nation

blocks.clueFragment: being so inadequate according to Edith
blocks.note: second meaning: what nurse Edith Cavell said was not enough before her execution

explanation.surface: Edith thinks countryside enthusiasts fall short.
explanation.walkthrough: Edith Cavell, a British nurse shot by the Germans in 1915, said 'Patriotism is not enough'. 'Country-lovers' suggests rambling but means loving one's nation.
explanation.definitionFit: A patriot loves their country, and Cavell said that quality alone was not enough.

clue.text: Flew home it was said in 1957

definitions.text: Flew home it was said in 1957

blocks.note: surface reading: someone took a plane back home
setter's reading: the flu of 1957 was named after its continent of origin, so 'flew' is said like 'flu'

explanation.surface: In 1957 someone reportedly took a flight home.
explanation.walkthrough: The 1957 pandemic was called Asian flu; the clue spells 'flu' as 'flew' and asks for where that flu was said to come from.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1957 influenza outbreak began in China and was named Asian flu, so the continent was taken as its home.

clue.text: Describing a short tale, can do with re-writing

definitions.text: Describing a short tale, can do with re-writing

indicators.note: rewriting means putting words down again in another form, so their letters are reordered

blocks.note: taken as written, used twice by the clue
taken as written

explanation.surface: A writer's story could be improved by a redraft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tale' does double duty: it ends the definition and also starts the anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Anecdotal means in the form of an anecdote, a brief personal story, so it describes such a short account.

clue.text: He's ambitious to tear up an entry in a way

indicators.note: in a down entry, 'up' means the word is read from bottom to top
making an entry into something puts it inside

blocks.note: taken as written
ST, the abbreviation for street, splits to hold the rest
to rip is to tear
taken as written
the end of the street abbreviation

explanation.surface: An ambitious man is out to rip up a competition form.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tear up' looks like destroying a form, but in a down clue 'up' means reading a word bottom to top. ST is the usual abbreviation for street, a way.
explanation.definitionFit: An aspirant is a person who aspires, who hopes and strives to achieve a high position.

clue.text: Play parts in the Bible

blocks.note: first meaning: the main divisions of a stage play
second meaning: the New Testament book after the four Gospels

explanation.surface: Taking roles in a Bible drama.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play parts' reads as acting roles, but it means the sections of a play.
explanation.definitionFit: A play is divided into acts, and the Acts of the Apostles is a New Testament book about the early church.

clue.text: Uttered quiet classical greeting in a plane

blocks.note: past tense of speak
the sound made to ask for quiet
Latin for hail

explanation.surface: A passenger whispered a Roman hello on an aircraft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plane' suggests an aircraft but is the carpenter's tool.
explanation.definitionFit: A spokeshave is a small woodworking plane with handles either side, used to shape curved pieces like wheel spokes.

clue.text: So test a candidate with a riddle

blocks.note: first meaning: to vet an applicant before appointment
second meaning: a coarse sieve for soil or gravel

explanation.surface: An interviewer tries out a job applicant with a puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Riddle' looks like a puzzle question, but it is a gardener's sieve, as is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To vet applicants is to screen them, and a screen is also a mesh for sifting soil, a riddle in that sense.

clue.text: Different actions taken by a holiday-maker

blocks.note: a suit is one kind of legal action
a case is another kind of legal action, different from the first word

explanation.surface: A tourist on holiday does all sorts of things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Different actions' asks for two separate words for a lawsuit, one after the other. The definition is a noun phrase: the thing taken by a holiday-maker.
explanation.definitionFit: A traveller packs clothes into luggage and carries it along, so the bag is something taken on holiday.

clue.text: What every well-informed conductor will know

definitions.text: What every well-informed conductor will know

blocks.note: surface reading: the knowing person is said to know how things stand, an idiom
setter's reading: the written music an orchestra's conductor must learn

explanation.surface: A well-informed bus conductor knows how things stand.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'know the score' is an idiom for being well-informed; a musical conductor knows it literally.
explanation.definitionFit: A score is the full written music showing every part, which a conductor studies before leading the orchestra.

clue.text: Girl cast off, ruined

blocks.note: short for Diana
to shed is to cast off, as a snake its skin

explanation.surface: A jilted girl is left devastated.
explanation.definitionFit: To dish someone is informal British for wrecking their hopes or plans, so dished means done for.

clue.text: Indication of suit shown by this on the sleeve?

definitions.text: shown by this on the sleeve?
definitions.note: a cryptic hint: feelings are shown by wearing this on the sleeve

blocks.note: first meaning: the symbol marking one of the four suits in a pack of cards

blocks.clueFragment: shown by this on the sleeve?
blocks.note: second meaning: what the idiom says an open person wears on their sleeve, showing their feelings

explanation.surface: A tailor's mark on the sleeve tells you whose suit it is.
explanation.walkthrough: To wear your heart on your sleeve is to show your feelings openly; a suit here is courtship and a card suit, not clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: The organ stands for love, so wearing it on the sleeve shows a suitor's feelings, and it is also a card suit.

clue.text: Anger rises about the Red

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: ire is anger
c for circa, about

explanation.surface: Anger mounts over a communist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Red' looks like a communist but completes the name of the Norse explorer who founded the first settlement in Greenland.
explanation.definitionFit: Eric the Red was the tenth-century Viking who settled Greenland, so 'the Red' is the epithet attached to his name.

clue.text: 28? Not in the Sappers

blocks.note: the opposite of in
the Royal Engineers, whose soldiers are nicknamed sappers

explanation.surface: Someone eccentric is no longer with the army engineers.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the answer to 28-across, ECCENTRIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Outré describes something unconventional and bizarre, beyond accepted bounds, just as odd behaviour is.

clue.text: Call silver worker a villain - in morality

blocks.note: to term something is to call it by a name
chemical symbol for silver
a worker ant

explanation.surface: A jeweller's employee is denounced as a moral villain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Morality' is short for a morality play, the medieval religious drama, where Termagant was a ranting imagined Muslim deity and stock villain.
explanation.definitionFit: Termagant was a violent, blustering idol in medieval mystery and morality plays, the source of today's word for a shrew.

clue.text: 25 receives two cents net change with this card

indicators.note: something that receives takes others in, so one word holds the rest inside
to change a word is to alter it, here by rearranging its letters

blocks.note: the answer to 25-down
c is the abbreviation for cent, twice
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Eric pockets a couple of cents' net change and plays a card.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Card' is not a playing card but an amusing, odd person; 'change' looks like coins but rearranges the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A card is an informal word for a comical or unusual character, someone delightfully odd in manner.

clue.text: Some say a small drink — a litre

definitions.note: 'Some' said aloud is 'sum', a noun for the answer

blocks.note: a tot is a small measure of spirits
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for litre

explanation.surface: Some people claim a small drink amounts to a litre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some say' reads as 'according to some people', but it is 'sum' pronounced, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A total is the sum of numbers added together, the figure at the foot of a column.
